title: Keyboard Manager shortcuts cannot override Windows shortcuts

judgment.rationale: The public reproduction proves a shell-hotkey conflict but cannot distinguish hook matching, suppression timing, injection failure, elevation, or settings state.
evidence: Win+Left and Win+Right mappings are reported to invoke Windows Snap.
Keyboard Manager already has a low-level hook and shortcut-to-key suppression path.
Related issues describe both shell-reserved and elevation-related failures.
No diagnostic archive or hook/injection trace is supplied.
judgment.recommended_action: Request a fresh diagnostic and a focused comparison matrix before approving a code design.

fix_assessment.rationale: A product fix may apply, but the failing boundary is not proven; retain a red provisional investigation plan rather than inventing a root cause.

proposed_fixes.title: Instrument and isolate Win+Arrow remapping before changing suppression
proposed_fixes.root_cause: Provisional: the shell may receive Win+Arrow because the low-level hook misses or suppresses the physical event too late, or because replacement input fails; current evidence cannot choose among these.
plan: Capture hook initialization, settings load, match detection, modifier restoration, SendInput result, and suppression return for Win+Arrow.
Compare normal and elevated PowerToys, Snap enabled/disabled, and a non-shell Win shortcut.
Only after the trace identifies the boundary, add a narrowly scoped suppression or deferred injection fix and matching tests.
verification: The diagnostic matrix identifies whether matching, suppression, or injection is failing before implementation begins.

confidence.rationale: The current code suggests several plausible mechanisms and the issue lacks the evidence needed to select one.

issue_context.summary: Keyboard Manager mappings for Win+Arrow do not prevent Windows Snap, but the report lacks the trace needed to identify where the remap path fails.
known_information: The report uses Win+Left to Home and Win+Right to End.
The actual result is Windows Snap left/right.
The affected versions include stable and preview builds on Windows 11.
Related issues cover shell-reserved shortcuts and elevation/UIPI behavior.
inferences: The defect may be specific to shell-reserved Win+Arrow handling rather than all shortcut-to-key mappings.
A deferred injection design is only one possible fix and must not be implemented without a trace.
issue_context.analysis: Local code contains a nominal suppression path and existing tests, so changing it blindly could regress other mappings. A fresh bug report plus a small controlled matrix can distinguish hook installation, shortcut matching, physical suppression, and SendInput failure.
initial_investigation: Inspected KeyboardManager::HookProc, HandleKeyboardHookEvent, KeyboardEventHandlers::HandleShortcutRemapEvent, Shortcut modifier checks, and OS-level remapping tests.
Reviewed related issues 26001 and 40012 for alternate failure classes.
Fork mirror Issue 638 records the provisional design and adversary determination.

information_gaps.information: A fresh PowerToys diagnostic archive captured immediately after reproducing Win+Arrow
information_gaps.why_needed: It can show hook initialization, settings load, and input injection errors.
information_gaps.how_to_collect: Reproduce once, then add a comment containing /bugreport immediately afterward.

information_gaps.information: Comparison of normal versus elevated PowerToys, Snap enabled versus disabled, and Win+Arrow versus Win+A
information_gaps.why_needed: It separates shell reservation and integrity-level failures from general remapping failures.
information_gaps.how_to_collect: Record the result for each case in a numbered comment on the issue.

design.root_cause: Not yet established. The leading alternatives are a low-level hook/match failure, physical Win+Arrow suppression occurring too late for the shell, or replacement input failure under shell/elevation conditions.
evidence: [Observed] The shell action occurs instead of the mapped Home/End key.
[Observed] Existing Keyboard Manager code returns suppression after a shortcut match and sends virtual input.
[Inferred] Instrumentation is required before selecting a safe code change.

affected_files.purpose: Installs the low-level hook and decides suppression.
Matches shortcuts and injects replacement keys.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: The code matches shortcuts, restores modifiers, injects replacement input, and returns suppression, but the failure point for Win+Arrow is unknown.
implementation_steps.change: Add temporary or test-gated diagnostics for match, modifier state, SendInput result, and return value; do not ship a behavioral change until the trace is reviewed.
edge_cases: Do not log sensitive text or leave verbose diagnostics enabled in production.
Preserve AltGr, repeat, elevation, and modifier restoration behavior.
tests: Extend existing tests with Win+Left/Right and both Win keys once the failing branch is known.

verify: Have the reporter reproduce and add `/bugreport` immediately afterward.
Run the four-case comparison matrix: normal/elevated and Snap on/off, plus Win+A control.
Inspect hook and SendInput diagnostics; only then finalize an implementation-grade fix.
Manual E2E must verify Home/End insertion and no Snap action in an interactive desktop.
risks: A guessed suppression change could break modifier state or repeat behavior.
Deferred injection could alter shortcut timing and elevation semantics.
alternatives: Declaring Win+Arrow unsupported conflicts with the current remapping expectation.
Blindly changing SendInput timing is unsafe without evidence.

mirror.fork_title: [Issue 50351] Keyboard Manager shortcuts cannot override Windows shortcuts

adversary.verdict: Blocking objection remains: evidence does not identify the failing boundary; request information.

comment.body: The Win+Arrow reproduction and mappings are useful, but the current code already has a low-level hook and suppression path, so the failure could be hook matching, shell timing, or replacement-input failure. Please reproduce once and add a comment containing `/bugreport` immediately afterward, then report results for normal versus elevated PowerToys, Windows Snap enabled versus disabled, and a control mapping such as Win+A. Those cases will identify the safe fix path.
